hook.core: It's 6 am. You've been sick all night and your shift starts at 9. Your manager has never seen you sick before. Do you text? Call? What do you even say? And what about the message from your manager last night at 10:30: do you have to answer it?

why.support: Lots of problems at work are about talking. A sick day nobody knew about. A swap that wasn't OK'd. A question you didn't ask. Know what to say, and you'll be trusted.
why.core: Most problems at work aren't about the work. They're about talk: a sick day nobody was told about, a shift swap that wasn't approved, a question you were too nervous to ask. Knowing what to say, how formal to be and when to put it in writing makes you the worker everyone trusts.
why.extend: Workplace communication runs on unwritten rules: how formal to be with whom, what must be in writing, and when you're expected to respond. Mastering them protects your job, your relationships and your rights, including the right not to be on call when you're not being paid.

articles.title: How to talk at work

body.support:
At work, how you say things matters. Four rules: be **early**, be **clear**, be **polite**, and get it **in writing**.

**Calling in sick.** Tell your manager **early**, before your shift. Say you're sick. Say when you'll be back. Some workplaces want a call, not a text.

**Swapping shifts.** Find someone to swap with. Then ask your manager to OK it. Keep the message.

**Asking questions.** Not sure? Ask! Then check: *So you want me to…?*

**Messaging your manager.** Say hi. Get to the point. Say thanks. No slang.

- To a mate: *cant come 2day sick*
- To a manager: *Hi Sarah, it's Jordan. I'm sick and can't come to my shift today. Sorry.*

When you're not at work, you usually don't have to answer work messages.
body.core:
At work, how you say something matters as much as what you say. Four rules cover most situations: be **early**, be **clear**, be **polite**, and get important things **in writing**.

**Calling in sick.** Tell your manager **as early as you can**, before your shift starts. Say who you are, that you're unwell and can't work, and when you think you'll be back. Follow your workplace's rules: many want a phone call, not a text. Your employer can ask for evidence, like a medical certificate, even for one day. (If you're **casual**, you usually don't get paid for sick days, but you still need to tell them.)

**Shift swaps.** Find a workmate who can take your shift first. Then ask your manager to **approve** the swap, and keep the reply. If it isn't approved and nobody turns up, it's your name on the roster.

**Asking questions.** Nobody expects a new worker to know everything. If you're not sure, ask. Then **check** you've got it: *Just to clarify, you want the tables wiped before the chairs go up?* It's much better than guessing wrong.

**Messaging your manager.** Use a greeting, get to the point, and say thanks. Save the slang, emojis and *lol* for your mates. Compare:

- *cant come 2day sick* (to a mate, fine)
- *Hi Sarah, it's Jordan. I'm unwell and can't make my 4 pm shift today. I expect to be back on Thursday. Sorry for the short notice.* (to a manager)

One more thing: Australian workers now have a **right to disconnect**. Outside your working hours, you can usually choose not to read or reply to work messages, unless refusing would be unreasonable.
body.extend:
Talking at work comes down to timing, clarity, tone and keeping records. Four principles cover most situations: **early**, **clear**, **polite** and **in writing**.

**Calling in sick.** Under Fair Work rules, you must tell your employer as soon as you reasonably can, ideally before the shift. Say you're unwell, you can't work, and when you expect to be back. Use the channel your workplace requires (often a call). Employers can ask for evidence, like a medical certificate, even for one day. **Casual** employees usually have no paid sick leave, but they still need to give notice.

**Shift swaps.** Arrange cover first, then seek your manager's approval, and keep the written confirmation. Until it's approved, the shift is still yours.

**Asking questions.** Clarifying is a professional skill, not a weakness. Say instructions back in your own words (*Just to clarify, you'd like…?*) to catch mistakes early.

**Messaging your manager.** Formality shows respect: a greeting, a clear purpose and a polite close. Language that's fine with mates (*cant come 2day*) reads very differently to the person who sets your shifts.

Finally, since 2024 Australian employees have had a **right to disconnect**. Outside working hours, they can refuse to read or reply to work contact, unless refusing is unreasonable.

caseStudies.title: The right to switch off

body.support:
Some bosses send messages late at night. Lots of workers felt they had to reply.

In **2024**, the law changed. Now there is a **right to disconnect**. It started in **2024** for most workplaces. It started in **2025** for small businesses.

It means: when you're not at work, you **don't have to reply** to work messages. Unless it would be unreasonable.

A text at 10:30 pm about tomorrow's shift? You can reply in the morning.

If there's a problem, talk to your boss first. The **Fair Work Commission** can help too.
body.core:
For years, lots of workers felt they had to answer their boss's messages any time: at dinner, late at night, on days off.

In **2024**, the law changed. Australia brought in a **right to disconnect**. It started on **26 August 2024** for most workplaces, and on **26 August 2025** for small businesses (those with fewer than 15 employees).

It means that outside your working hours, you can **refuse to read or reply** to work calls, messages and emails, **unless refusing would be unreasonable**.

What's unreasonable depends on things like why they're contacting you, how urgent it is, whether you're paid to be available, and your role. A message at 10:30 pm asking you to cover tomorrow's shift? You can reply in the morning. A real emergency might be different.

The **Fair Work Ombudsman** says the first step is for workers and employers to talk it through. If that doesn't work, the **Fair Work Commission** can help sort it out.
body.extend:
Smartphones blurred the line between work and home for many workers. Messages arrived at dinner, late at night and on days off, with an unspoken expectation of a quick reply.

In **2024**, federal Parliament added a **right to disconnect** to the *Fair Work Act*. It began on **26 August 2024** for most employers. It reached small businesses (fewer than 15 employees) on **26 August 2025**.

Outside working hours, employees may **refuse to read or reply** to work contact, unless refusing is **unreasonable**. That depends on things like how urgent the contact is, whether the worker is paid to be on call, their role and their situation.

The Fair Work Ombudsman encourages workers and employers to sort out disagreements at work first. If they can't, the **Fair Work Commission** can help.

The law shows that workplace communication carries power: who can contact whom, when, and whether they expect an answer.

teacher.overview: Students learn the everyday talk of a workplace: calling in sick, arranging and getting approval for shift swaps, asking and clarifying questions, and messaging a manager at the right level of formality. They study the right to disconnect (in force from 2024, and for small businesses from 2025), write three workplace messages and role-play a sick call.
prep: Find out which students have jobs. They're your experts on how their workplace handles sick calls and swaps (apps, group chats, calls).
Optional: invite a local employer or a manager from a fast food or retail chain to say what they wish new workers knew.
Note: Make the Call covers phone call structure; this course is about workplace relationships and messages.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — The four rules
steps: **Hook (10 min):** the 6 am sick scenario. Students write what they'd send, then compare.
**Explicit teaching (10 min):** early, clear, polite, in writing; model a sick message and a swap message.
**Read (15 min):** article and Check your reading.
**Annotate (10 min):** Anatomy of a shift-swap message.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Formality
steps: **Fix the message (15 min).** Read rewrites aloud.
**What would you say? (20 min):** in pairs, act out each scenario.
**Exit (5 min):** one clarifying sentence you'll use.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Rights and messages
steps: **Case study (20 min):** the right to switch off. Discuss what's unreasonable.
**Exit (5 min):** swap and check a partner's sick message.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Role-play
steps: **Role-play it (20 min):** sick calls in pairs, then swap.

keyPoints: Calling in sick: before your shift; you're unwell, can't work, when you'll be back; evidence if asked. Casuals usually aren't paid for sick days.
Shift swaps: find cover first, then get approval, and keep it.
Clarify instructions by repeating them back.
Right to disconnect: outside working hours, you can usually choose not to reply, unless that's unreasonable.

teacher.answers:
**Four rules:** early, clear, polite, in writing. Sick call: you're unwell and can't work, and when you'll be back (and who you are). Find cover first so the manager only has to approve. Right to disconnect: outside working hours you can usually refuse to read or reply to work contact unless that's unreasonable.

**Swap message:** 1 greeting; 2 who; 3 the request with exact times; 4 cover sorted; 5 short reason; 6 close asking for approval.

**Sort:** sick emoji — mate; Hi Sarah unwell — manager; yo take my sat — mate; could I please swap — manager; thanks for the till — manager; boss was stressed — mate.

**Fix the message (samples):** *Hi Sarah, could you please confirm what time I start on Saturday? Thanks, Jordan.* / *Hi Sarah, I can't make my Saturday shift. I'm asking around for someone to cover and will let you know.* / *Hi Sarah, I'm stuck in traffic and will be about 15 minutes late. Sorry.*

**Case study reply (sample):** *Hi Sarah, sorry, I only just saw this. I can't do 7 am today, but I'm free from 12 if that helps.*

Fair Work Ombudsman — Notice and medical certificates

realityCheck: **Workplaces differ.** Many use rostering apps or group chats; some insist on a phone call. Teach the principles and tell students to follow their workplace's rules.
**Students with jobs are gold.** Ask them how their workplace handles sick calls and swaps, and what went wrong for them early on.

**Some students face unfair treatment at work.** If a student describes being pressured, underpaid or unsafe, point them to the Fair Work Ombudsman or the Young Workers Centre, and follow your school's wellbeing process.
**The right to disconnect has limits.** It's not a right to ignore your boss: refusal can be unreasonable. Keep the nuance.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's quick, practical and immediately useful for any student with a casual job.
